summary: Gives network operators advice on deploying 6to4, an automatic technique for tunneling IPv6 over IPv4. It is aimed at ISPs, including those that do not yet support IPv6, and at content providers, with some advice for implementers. The goal is fewer unhappy users and help-desk calls.

plainLanguage.summary: 6to4 carries IPv6 packets across an IPv4 network by wrapping them in IPv4 packets. This RFC explains why those tunnels can fail and what network operators can do to handle them.

subtitle: Operational advice for networks where automatic IPv6-over-IPv4 tunnels are present.

tldr.problem: 6to4 can provide IPv6 connectivity over an IPv4 network, but real deployments can fail in ways that are difficult for users and operators to diagnose.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes how router and anycast 6to4 work, examines observed failure modes, and gives advice to equipment vendors, ISPs, transit networks, and content providers.
tldr.outcome: This Informational guidance is intended to reduce connectivity failures and support problems where 6to4 is already in use.

today: RFC 6343 is an Informational document published in August 2011. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why the RFC Gives 6to4 Advice
sections.content:
6to4 is an automatic way to carry IPv6 traffic across an IPv4 network. The RFC describes two forms: a router can use another configured 6to4 router, or a host can use the anycast relay address defined for 6to4.

Some systems and home routers had 6to4 enabled without the user choosing it. When a tunnel fails, the user may see delays or failed connections without knowing that 6to4 is involved. This document advises operators and implementers on those deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: 6to4 lets IPv6 traffic cross an IPv4 network. When a tunnel fails, users may not know why their connection is slow or unavailable.

sections.title: How Router and Anycast 6to4 Work
sections.content:
A 6to4 router uses its global IPv4 address to form an IPv6 prefix. It sends IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets using protocol number 41. A relay can remove that outer IPv4 packet and forward the IPv6 packet into a native IPv6 network.

In router 6to4, the site configures a relay. Anycast 6to4 uses the IPv4 address 192.88.99.1 as the default relay address, avoiding that configuration at the user site. The outgoing and return packets do not have to pass through the same relay.
sections.plainLanguage: A 6to4 router puts an IPv6 packet inside an IPv4 packet and sends it to a relay. The relay removes the outer packet and forwards the IPv6 packet.

sections.title: Failure Modes and Operator Guidance
sections.content:
The RFC reports connection failures linked to blocked protocol 41 traffic, missing or unwilling return relays, routing problems, and packet-size problems. A tunnel can also fail when an address used by 6to4 has no working return route. Such failures can be hard to diagnose because IPv4 connections may still work.

The advice depends on the operator's role. Vendors should not enable 6to4 by default. Operators should check whether relays work and whether their networks pass the required traffic. Networks that provide native IPv6 are advised to direct users to that service rather than 6to4.
sections.plainLanguage: Firewalls, routing, or packet sizes can stop a 6to4 connection. Operators should check their relays and avoid turning 6to4 on for users without their choice.

sections.title: Security and Managed Tunnels
sections.content:
The RFC notes that tunneling can hide an inner packet from security devices that inspect only the outer packet. A well-managed relay can provide a defined point where the packet is visible as ordinary IPv6 traffic and security measures can be applied.

Blocking protocol 41 everywhere is not compatible with the RFC's approach to reducing 6to4 problems. The document also describes provider-managed tunnel options, while noting that protocol 41 and IPv6 Path MTU Discovery still need appropriate handling.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel can hide the carried packet from devices that inspect only the outside packet. Operators need to consider security and packet-size handling at the tunnel endpoints.
